 A hacking group calling itself ScarlettGroup has claimed that it breached AU Small Finance Bank and stole sensitive customer and internal data. The group has also threatened to publish the material online.   The claim was first flagged by the cybersecurity monitoring account @H4ckmanac on X. According to the post, the attackers say they gained access to know your customer (KYC) records and personal identification documents belonging to customers, including Permanent Account Number (PAN) and Aadhaar details. The alleged haul goes well beyond basic identity information. The group says it holds credit reports, bank statements, loan applications and signed agreements. It also lists insurance-related records and customer relationship management (CRM) data, along with internal material such as employee details, login histories and audit logs. The post did not specify how much data is involved, and the list is the group’s own description rather than a verified inventory.   What the bank has said AU Small Finance Bank has not given any official statement on the incident. It has neither confirmed the breach nor responded to the claims. The authenticity of the data and the extent of any compromise have not been independently established, so the claims remain to be verified.   What trackers show According to a report published on Threxar , the ransomware-tracking site Ransomware.live recorded on 29 October 2026 that the domain au.bank.in had been claimed by ScarlettGroup, which the site flags as a new group. The same report cites a tracking blog, which said the group’s leak page for the bank carries a negotiation countdown and that the bank had only asked people to contact it by direct message. The report’s authors could not independently confirm that detail, which comes from a secondary source. They also said they had not seen any published sample of the data and could not verify whether any of it has been released.   Who is ScarlettGroup The report describes ScarlettGroup as a recent arrival. The security firm Foresiet documented it in a report published on 21 October 2026, saying the group began appearing in threat-monitoring records around September and became more visible in October.   Foresiet describes an extortion operation built on public pressure. The group runs a leak site on The Onion Router (Tor) network that lists alleged victims with industry labels and countdown timers. Its stated process has three stages: public listing, a negotiation window, and then closure or disclosure. The group says a settlement leads to the listing being removed and the data deleted, while failure to settle may lead to publication. Foresiet cautions that there is no independent guarantee the data would actually be deleted after any payment.   Researchers also point to what remains unknown. The reporting does not establish how the group gets into networks, whether it encrypts files, or how many victims it has. Foresiet says the listings so far have covered technology, education, government and entertainment, and that it has documented activity on the PwnForums site. Reported links to other forums still need verification.   A mixed track record Two earlier ScarlettGroup claims show why this one is hard to judge, according to the report. The group claimed an attack on the contact-centre software company Genesys, which later disclosed that its own internal learning-management and CRM systems had been accessed. Genesys said its Genesys Cloud and Engage products were not compromised, and it did not name an attacker, so the link to ScarlettGroup rests on the group’s own claim.   The second claim concerned Rajasthan Police. On 21 October 2026, Business Today reported that the group claimed about 70,000 identity records and 59,460 mobile numbers from the force, along with First Information Report (FIR) and witness material. A Deputy Inspector General (DIG) of cyber later said the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) had been informed, but reports noted that authorities had not independently confirmed the extent of the breach. In short, the group has made claims that coincided with a real incident and others that remain unconfirmed. A claim naming a company is not proof of a breach, but this group’s claims cannot be dismissed out of hand either.   Why the claim matters If the claim turns out to be genuine, the exposure could leave customers open to identity theft, loan fraud and other scams aimed at account holders. KYC documents combined with financial records are the raw material for impersonation. Should the data be released, it could be used to open fraudulent accounts, take out loans in someone else’s name, or run convincing phishing campaigns that quote real financial details.   What the bank would be expected to do If AU Small Finance Bank confirms unauthorised access, it would be required to report the incident to the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) within hours of detecting it, according to the report. The new data protection law carries heavier penalties, but most of its duties are not scheduled to apply until around May 2027, so the immediate pressure on the bank is more likely to come from CERT-In and RBI rules.   What customers should do Customers have been advised to stay alert to suspicious calls, messages and emails, including WhatsApp messages, that mention their AU account, loan or card, even if the caller knows personal details, since correct details are no longer proof of identity. They should not share their PAN, Aadhaar, banking passwords, PINs, one-time passwords (OTPs) or other personal details with anyone who contacts them first. They should check statements and loan accounts for transactions or credit enquiries they do not recognise, and review their credit report for loans they did not take.   Customers should rely on official channels only, checking the bank’s own website or app for notices and calling the number printed on their card or passbook rather than one sent to them. Financial cyber fraud can be reported on the national cybercrime helpline 1930 or at cybercrime.gov.in. Those worried about misuse can also consider locking their Aadhaar biometrics through the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI) services.   What to watch next The key questions remain open. It is not yet clear whether AU Small Finance Bank will confirm an incident and, if so, what was accessed. It is also unknown whether ScarlettGroup will publish a verifiable sample when its countdown ends, or whether CERT-In or the RBI will say anything on the matter.
